correctness.rationale: Independently checked the degree and count argument. Even parts and both top-degree odd parts are free, giving q^34; the commutator is twice the sum of the degree-(1,1) and degree-(1,3)/(3,1) wedge products. For leading vectors spanning S, the degree-four image is the kernel of the exterior quotient to Λ^4(V/S), so its dimension is 0, 4 or 5 according as dim S is 0, 1 or 2. The domain of the degree-four equation has dimension 20. A prescribed nonzero degree-two target fixes a two-plane and area, realized by (q²−1)q ordered bases: q²−1 possible first vectors, then q solutions to the area equation for the second vector. This yields the stated (q²−1)q^50 fiber for all degree-four targets. When the leading wedge vanishes, each nonzero leading pair spans a unique line, with q²−1 pairs per line. At a nonzero four-form only the lines in its four-dimensional wedge-annihilator are allowed, whereas all lines and the zero leading pair contribute when both target components vanish. The determinant-one count, Gaussian-binomial image count and mass q^64 check the exponents; this argument uses only invertibility of 2 and applies to all odd prime powers. The frozen code was inspected, not run: representative fiber totals are asserted at q=3, not at q=5; the q=5 loop is selected-pair sampling with repeat entries and the q=9 test is conservation only. None is needed for the universal proof.
residual_risks: No conclusion for characteristic two by the divided-target argument, other numbers of generators, or the graded bracket.

value.rationale: This is the complete distribution of a canonical map on a classical finite algebra, not a single representative or a recount of commuting pairs. Five generators allow nondecomposable leading targets while independent leading vectors already span all fourth-form output directions. The evaluated multiplicities exhibit a distinct hyperplane-incidence stratum at pure nonzero degree four, giving a useful exact baseline for additive commutator distributions.
residual_risks: The result is dimension-specific; it gives neither the fibers in larger exterior algebras nor the distribution for sums of brackets.
